domain: Thoracic anesthesia (one-lung ventilation, thoracic epidural, hypoxia during OLV, pneumonectomy/lobectomy, mediastinal mass, HPV)
stem: What does MAC-amnesia represent in relation to standard MAC for volatile anesthetics?
answer: MAC-amnesia is the concentration preventing recall in 50% of patients, which is lower than MAC-immobility (approximately 0.55 MAC)
rationale: Amnesia requires lower anesthetic depth than movement suppression; this distinguishes consciousness suppression from anti-nociceptive effects.
confusable_with: MAC-awake (concentration at which 50% respond to verbal command, also below standard MAC)

domain: Thoracic anesthesia (one-lung ventilation, thoracic epidural, hypoxia during OLV, pneumonectomy/lobectomy, mediastinal mass, HPV)
stem: What five causes of hypoxemia are differentiated by alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient calculation?
answer: Low inspired O2, diffusion impairment, V/Q mismatch, shunt (V/Q=0), hypoventilation - differentiated by A-a gradient and response to supplemental O2
rationale: Shunt does not correct with 100% O2 (distinguishing it from V/Q mismatch); diffusion impairment and low FiO2 correct easily; hypoventilation raises CO2.
confusable_with: Shunt and V/Q mismatch being interchangeable (shunt uniquely unresponsive to O2)

domain: Thoracic anesthesia (one-lung ventilation, thoracic epidural, hypoxia during OLV, pneumonectomy/lobectomy, mediastinal mass, HPV)
stem: In the aged patient, what principal pharmacodynamic change reduces anesthetic requirement?
answer: Reduced anesthetic requirement (lower MAC) with aging due to reduced pharmacodynamic sensitivity
rationale: Neuronal density decreases with age and CNS sensitivity to anesthetic agents increases, requiring lower concentrations for equivalent effect.
confusable_with: Pharmacokinetic changes as the primary driver of MAC reduction with age (both contribute but pharmacodynamic change is principal)

domain: Thoracic anesthesia (one-lung ventilation, thoracic epidural, hypoxia during OLV, pneumonectomy/lobectomy, mediastinal mass, HPV)
stem: In obstetric patients, why does apnea develop faster than in non-pregnant patients during induction?
answer: Decreased FRC and increased oxygen uptake (higher metabolic rate) in pregnancy cause rapid oxygen desaturation during apnea
rationale: Reduced FRC means less oxygen reserve, and higher metabolic O2 consumption depletes that reserve faster, narrowing the safe apnea window.
confusable_with: Pregnancy reducing drug clearance as the primary risk (pharmacokinetics matter but the hypoxemia mechanism is physiological)

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: What is the key principle of sedation vacation (spontaneous awakening trials) in the ICU?
answer: Daily sedation interruptions (sedation vacation) improve outcomes by reducing total sedation dose and facilitating earlier liberation from ventilation
rationale: Continuous sedation accumulates drug burden and prolongs ICU stay; daily awakening trials allow assessment of neurological status and reduce time on ventilator.
confusable_with: Continuous deep sedation being safer for all intubated patients

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: What is the general postoperative management principle after pneumonectomy regarding mechanical ventilation?
answer: Most patients are extubated shortly after pneumonectomy to decrease postoperative morbidity
rationale: Early extubation after pneumonectomy reduces ventilator-associated complications and allows earlier mobilisation, which improves recovery.
confusable_with: Routine prolonged mechanical ventilation after all pneumonectomies

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: What analgesic approach is defined as a broad combination of interventional and systemic techniques that reduce opioid requirements?
answer: Multimodal analgesia: combination of regional techniques (epidural, peripheral nerve blocks) plus systemic non-opioid analgesics to reduce opioid burden
rationale: Targeting multiple analgesic pathways simultaneously reduces opioid side effects while maintaining or improving pain control.
confusable_with: High-dose opioid monotherapy as the gold standard for ICU analgesia

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: What unique opioid technique delivers substantially lower total opioid doses with fewer systemic side effects compared to systemic administration?
answer: Epidural and intrathecal opioids provide analgesia with substantially lower total doses and fewer systemic side effects than parenteral administration
rationale: Spinal delivery of opioids acts directly on dorsal horn receptors with minimal systemic uptake, achieving analgesia at a fraction of the systemic dose.
confusable_with: IV PCA being equivalent to neuraxial opioids in dose-sparing (neuraxial uses significantly lower doses)

domain: Anesthesia critical care (shock & resuscitation, sepsis, ARDS & mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic monitoring, AKI, sedation/delirium, nutrition, end-of-life)
stem: What medication class used in pain management should be withheld preoperatively or used with caution in patients with obstructive sleep apnea due to risk of apnea?
answer: Opioids and sedating medications (benzodiazepines) that cause upper airway obstruction or apnea should be withheld or used cautiously in OSA patients
rationale: OSA patients have baseline upper airway instability; opioids reduce upper airway muscle tone and blunt hypoxic arousal, dramatically increasing apnea risk.
confusable_with: All analgesics being contraindicated in OSA (non-opioid analgesics are safe)
